beats.beat: Mrs Hale, at the draper's window, sees Rowe and Judith return together at dusk, unchaperoned and laughing, and has the whole parish informed by morning.
Mrs Pike hears it first as triumph, assuming it confirms an attachment, then realizes with horror it is Judith spoken of, and not Louisa.
Flustered, Mrs Pike tells three separate people it was nothing at all, which naturally convinces everyone it was something.
Judith hears an invented version of the story, that she was seen weeping on Rowe's arm, from a girl at the library counter, and goes home changed in temper.
Owen Vane hears it from a customer, closes his shop early, and walks straight to the curate's lodging.

turn.note: Owen's declaration that he will demand an answer from Rowe about Judith's name directly sets up chapter 6's opening beat.

problems: The opening sentence mixes present tense ('looks north up the lane') with the past-tense narration ('had been at it since the coach came in'), an unmotivated tense shift a listener will catch.

trope_note: Serves the meddling matchmaker (her scheme misfires on itself) and the chaperone's absence (the unwitnessed hour now costs a reputation) strongly; enemies of manner is dormant this chapter, which is appropriate since it belongs to the gossip machinery rather than to Rowe and Judith directly.
fixes: The chapter runs noticeably over its 560-word target; trim 'She had sent them off herself.' from the Mrs Pike paragraph, which restates a fact already dramatized in Chapter 4.
Fix the opening sentence's tense: 'The library window looks north up the lane' should be past tense ('The library window looked north up the lane') to match the rest of the paragraph.

Consider tightening the Owen/Judith exchange at the end — several one- and two-word lines ('Get your tea.' / 'Owen.') are effective but could be compressed by one beat without losing the confrontation's snap, to help bring the chapter closer to target length.

findings.note: 3 clauses coordinated in 37 words. Heard once, the last one lands with the subject of the first already gone. Split after the first clause, or make every member the same grammatical shape so the ear can follow the pattern.

findings.quote: The younger Barrow girl was minding the counter, and lowered her voice, and said it must have been dreadful to be seen crying on the curate'...
findings.note: 42 words in one sentence. A listener cannot re-read it. Split it, or cut it to under 40.

writer_note:
This story is now read by a single narrator rather than a
cast with a voice each, so the prose has to carry who is speaking. It was
written under the old rule, which forbade attribution because the voices made it
redundant.

Go through the chapter and add attribution wherever a listener — who cannot see
the page, and cannot look back — would lose track of who is speaking. A tag
belongs in its own narrator segment: `said Mrs Pike`, `Rowe said`, or an action
that does the same work: *Rowe turned the note over.* Two people alternating in
a plain exchange do not need one every line; the third turn usually does, and so
does every return to dialogue after narration, and every line in a scene of
three or more.

Do not attribute every line. An unbroken column of `said X` is padding, and it
is the opposite failure.

Where a line would be misread without it, you may add a `tag` to that segment —
`"[quietly]"`, `"[a beat]"`, `"[warmly]"` — as performance direction for the
voice. It is never printed and never spoken. A few a chapter at most, and never
to imitate a different person: one voice reads everyone.

Come back no longer than you started. These chapters are already at or over
their word ceiling, and attribution adds words — so take them back out of
restatement: a line of dialogue that lands followed by narration explaining that
it landed, a room established twice. If you come back long the check sends the
chapter straight back to be cut, which spends a revision on arithmetic instead
of on the prose.

Change nothing else. Same events, same beats, same jokes, same last line.
